claims.text: The target alloy is Co-free FeNiCrMn derived from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
The as-solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy is a single-phase solid solution.
The dynamic tensile behavior of the alloy is governed by a temperature- and strain-rate-mediated shift in dislocation mechanisms.
Higher temperatures or lower strain rates increase thermally activated dislocation mobility.
Greater dislocation mobility permits dislocation rearrangement and dynamic recovery.
Dynamic recovery lowers the strain-hardening rate.
Lower temperatures or higher strain rates restrict dislocation motion.
Restricted dislocation motion causes accumulation, entanglement, and a dense network of pinned dislocations.
Dislocation accumulation and entanglement increase strain hardening.
Relative to room-temperature, high-strain-rate deformation, elevated-temperature or low-strain-rate specimens will have lower peak strength.
Relative to the baseline, elevated-temperature or low-strain-rate specimens will have lower strain-hardening rates.
Elevated-temperature or low-strain-rate specimens will exhibit lower dislocation density and more microstructural evidence of dynamic recovery.
Dislocation accumulation predominates at the room-temperature, high-strain-rate baseline.
In situ neutron diffraction can monitor lattice-strain evolution during elevated-temperature deformation of a single-phase HEA.
In situ neutron diffraction can quantify dislocation density under the proposed test conditions.
Tensile tests will vary temperature from room temperature to about 700°C and strain rate from 10^-4 to 10^-2 s^-1 while avoiding phase transformations or precipitation.
Failure to observe either the predicted mechanical-property trend or the predicted transition toward mobility and recovery would falsify the hypothesis.
